 NRS sets November 30 tax registration deadline for crypto firms
 Nigeria’s cryptocurrency exchanges and other virtual asset service providers (VASPs) have until November 30, 2026, to register with the Nigerian
 Ayomide Odunlami 
 November 19, 2026 
 3 min read 
 Listen to this article 
 Share 
 Nigeria’s cryptocurrency exchanges and other virtual asset service providers (VASPs) have until November 30, 2026, to register with the Nigerian Revenue Service (NRS), as the government steps up efforts to bring digital asset transactions within its tax administration system.
 Advertisement Advertisement The tax authority has also directed operators to integrate their systems with its newly deployed VASP Tax Portal by December 31, 2026, a second requirement intended to facilitate transaction reporting, tax assessment and the remittance of applicable taxes.
 In a public notice, the NRS said the requirements apply to Nigerian and foreign businesses providing virtual asset services to Nigerian residents, irrespective of their physical location. Failure to meet either deadline could attract statutory penalties and other enforcement measures.
 The development marks another step in Nigeria’s efforts to strengthen oversight of the cryptocurrency industry, following the introduction of new virtual asset tax guidelines in August, which provide for a 1.5 percent stamp duty on token-to-fiat and fiat-to-token transfers.
 The new registration framework covers cryptocurrency exchanges, peer-to-peer platforms, brokers, custodial wallet providers, payment and remittance companies, and other businesses involved in transferring, exchanging or safeguarding digital assets. 
 Under the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025, and the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025, operators are subject to tax obligations covering registration, record-keeping, reporting, filing and payment.
 Advertisement Section 79 and the Fifth Schedule of the tax administration law establish the obligations for persons engaged in virtual asset activities, while Section 71 provides the legal basis for deploying technology to automate tax administration.
 Two-stage registration process
 The NRS has divided the registration process into two stages, requiring operators to submit their business information through the portal by November 30 before completing technical integration by December 31.
 Advertisement The initial registration requires providers to supply their business details, Tax Identification Number (TIN), contact information, details of their virtual asset activities and relevant anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing registration information.
 The second stage involves integrating their systems with the NRS portal. The authority said detailed reporting requirements and application programming interface specifications would be provided during the technical integration process. Advertisement Advertisement 
 The integration is expected to enable the tax authority to receive transaction information, assess tax liabilities and facilitate the remittance of taxes collected in digital tokens.
 The NRS stressed that completing the initial registration alone would not satisfy the requirement, as operators would only be considered registered after completing both stages.
 The portal will also support the administration of existing tax obligations, including Value Added Tax (VAT), Stamp Duty and Withholding Tax payable in tokens. These functions will be introduced in phases, while taxes payable in fiat currency will continue to be administered through the existing Rev360 platform and other channels.
 The authority said the portal does not introduce additional taxes, but provides a framework for administering existing obligations under Nigerian tax laws.
 Providers remain responsible for taxes arising from their own taxable activities and, where applicable, for collecting or withholding taxes on customer transactions. 
 Tax registration separate from operating licence
 The NRS clarified that registration on the portal does not grant operators permission to provide virtual asset services in Nigeria, separating tax compliance from the licensing requirements of other financial regulators.
 The process is distinct from approvals administered by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) and other relevant authorities. This means operators must still obtain the necessary licences for their activities, even after completing their tax registration.
 The authority said it could share information collected through the portal with relevant regulators and law enforcement agencies where permitted by law, while information processed through the platform would remain subject to applicable data protection requirements.
 Individuals using virtual assets for personal purposes are excluded from the registration requirement, as are businesses that merely accept cryptocurrency as payment for their own goods and services. Their existing tax obligations, however, remain unchanged.
 By requiring operators to integrate directly with its reporting infrastructure, the NRS is extending its capacity to monitor taxable activity in the digital asset market, while making compliance a formal requirement for businesses serving Nigerian customers.
